entry: Organism that eats mostly or exclusively animal tissue. The term derives from the Latin *caro*, "flesh," and *vorare*, "to devour." Carnivores meet their energy and nutrient needs by consuming animal muscle, fat and other soft tissues, through predation or scavenging. Obligate carnivores, or hypercarnivores, derive more than 70% of their diet from meat and depend on animal flesh in the wild; cats, for example, appear unable to synthesize essential nutrients such as taurine. Mesocarnivores obtain 30–70% of their diet from meat, and hypocarnivores less than 30%. Dietary carnivory is not a distinguishing trait of the order [[Carnivora]]: most bear species are omnivorous, and cetaceans are highly carnivorous but are not carnivorans. Outside the animal kingdom, [[Carnivorous plant|carnivorous plants]] and fungi also exist. A carnivore at the top of a food chain is an [[Apex predator|apex predator]].

Plants that consume animals. Carnivorous plants derive some or most of their nutrients from trapping and digesting animals or protozoans, typically insects and other arthropods, and occasionally small mammals and birds. They grow in sunny, waterlogged places with thin, nutrient-poor soil, such as acidic [[Bog|bogs]], and are found on all continents except [[Antarctica]] and on many Pacific islands. In 1875, [[Charles Darwin]] published *Insectivorous Plants*, the first treatise to recognize the significance of carnivory in plants. True carnivory is believed to have evolved independently at least 12 times in five orders of flowering plants. Five basic trapping mechanisms are found: pitfall, flypaper, snap, bladder and lobster-pot traps. [[Venus flytrap|Venus flytraps]], pitcher plants and bladderworts exemplify key traits of carnivory, and at least 800 species are known.

Evergreen legume tree or shrub native to the Mediterranean region and the Middle East. Carob (*Ceratonia siliqua*) is widely cultivated for its edible seed pods and as an ornamental tree. Spain is its largest producer, followed by Italy and Morocco. The pods are made into a powder or chips that serve as a [[Chocolate|chocolate]] alternative. The seeds yield locust bean gum, or carob gum, a thickener used in food processing. The word derives via French from Arabic *kharrūb*, "locust bean pod."

American comedienne, actress, singer and writer. Burnett starred in *The Carol Burnett Show*, a variety-sketch series on [[CBS]] that ran from 1967 to 1978. She was the first woman to host a comedy-variety series, and the show won numerous Emmy and Golden Globe Awards. Her film roles include *The Front Page* (1974) and *Annie* (1982). She has received five Golden Globe Awards, seven Primetime Emmy Awards and a Grammy Award, and was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2005.

American singer-songwriter and musician. With her first husband, lyricist Gerry Goffin, King composed over two dozen hit songs for various artists in the 1960s. She wrote or co-wrote 118 songs that charted on the Billboard Hot 100. Her solo album *Tapestry* (1971) topped the U.S. album chart for 15 weeks. King has sold over 75 million records worldwide. Her honors include four [[Grammy Awards]], induction into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] twice, and the 2013 Gershwin Prize for Popular Song from the [[Library of Congress]], the first awarded to a woman.

Extremely hot cultivar of the *Capsicum chinense* pepper plant. American breeder Ed Currie began working on it around 2001, and the name "reaper" refers to the sickle-like shape of its tail. [[Guinness World Records]] listed it as the hottest chili pepper from 2013 to 2023, and certified an average of 1,641,183 SHU (Scoville heat units) in 2017. It was surpassed by Pepper X, also developed by Currie, which was tested at an average of 2.69 million SHU.

German-born British astronomer. Between 1786 and 1797 she discovered eight comets, including the periodic comet 35P/Herschel–Rigollet, and independently detected several nebulae. She was the younger sister of [[William Herschel]], with whom she worked for most of her career. Born in [[Hanover]], she spent 50 years in England before returning to Germany in 1822. She was the first professional female astronomer and the first woman to receive a salary as a scientist. She was also the first woman to publish scientific findings in the *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society* and the first woman awarded a Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society (1828).

Frankish-dominated empire in Western and Central Europe (800–888). The Carolingian dynasty had ruled as kings of the [[Franks]] since 751. In 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charles the Great, better known as [[Charlemagne]], as Roman emperor. The empire's heartland was [[Francia]], between the Loire and the Rhine, and [[Aachen]] was Charlemagne's primary residence. After a civil war from 840 to 843 following the death of Emperor [[Louis the Pious]], the empire was divided into autonomous kingdoms. [[Charles the Fat]] reunited them in 884, but he was deposed in 887, and the empire dissolved. Its population was roughly between 10 and 20 million.

American actress of television and film. Jones played Morticia Addams in the television sitcom *The Addams Family* from 1964. She was nominated for an [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Supporting Actress for *The Bachelor Party* (1957). She shared a Golden Globe Award for New Star of the Year–Actress for *Marjorie Morningstar*. Her films include *House of Wax* (1953) and *King Creole* (1958), in which she appeared with [[Elvis Presley]].

Class of yellow, orange or red organic pigments. Carotenoids are produced by plants, algae, several bacteria, archaea and fungi. More than 1,100 carotenoids have been identified, falling into two classes: xanthophylls, which contain oxygen, and carotenes, which are purely hydrocarbons. All are tetraterpenoids made from eight isoprene units, with 40 carbon atoms. They absorb light at wavelengths of 400 to 550 nm, which produces their color. In plants and algae, carotenoids absorb light energy for [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] and provide photoprotection. Carotenes including β-carotene and α-carotene have vitamin A activity, as they can be converted to retinol. Carotenoids are the dominant pigment in the autumn leaf coloration of about 15–30% of tree species.

Common name for numerous species of freshwater fish in the family Cyprinidae. Cyprinidae is a large family of ray-finned fish mostly native to [[Eurasia]], and carp are prized as food and ornamental fish in much of the Old World. They are considered trash fish and invasive pests in many parts of Africa, Australia and most of the United States. The common carp (*Cyprinus carpio*), native to Eastern Europe and Western Asia, is sometimes called the "Eurasian" carp. Goldfish and koi, a domesticated variety of common carp, are popular ornamental fishes. Several carp species are considered [[Invasive species|invasive]] in the United States, and worldwide large sums are spent on carp control. At least some species survive for months with practically no [[Oxygen|oxygen]] by converting [[Glycogen|glycogen]] to [[Lactic acid|lactic acid]], which is then converted into [[Ethanol|ethanol]] and [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]]; the ethanol diffuses through the gills into the surrounding water.

Mountain range forming an arc across Central and Southeast Europe. Roughly 1,500 km long, the range is the third-longest European mountain range, after the Urals and the [[Scandinavian Mountains]]. It stretches from the Western Carpathians in Austria, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary and Poland, through the Eastern Carpathians in Poland, Slovakia, [[Ukraine]] and Romania, to the Southern Carpathians in Romania and Serbia. The highest peaks, in the Tatra Mountains, exceed 2,600 m. The Carpathians provide habitat for the largest European populations of brown bears, wolves, chamois and lynxes. Romania has the second-largest area of virgin forest in Europe, after [[Russia]].

Genus of ants (*Camponotus*) found nearly worldwide except in Antarctica and a few islands. It is the most species-rich ant genus, with over 1,500 described species. Although all are commonly called carpenter ants, only a few members nest in wood. They chew galleries out of dead, damp wood and discard a sawdust-like material rather than eating the wood. Their tunneling is a major cause of structural damage to wooden buildings, although it also aids forest [[Decomposition|decomposition]]. The ants farm [[Aphid|aphids]], protecting them from predators while collecting the honeydew they excrete. Most species forage at night, collecting dead insects and honeydew. Colonies often include a central parent colony surrounded by smaller satellite colonies.

Skilled trade in which building materials are cut, shaped and installed. Carpenters traditionally worked with natural wood, and the trade includes construction of buildings, ships, timber bridges and concrete formwork. Until the end of the 19th century, carpenters normally framed post-and-beam buildings, a method now called timber framing. Apprenticeships usually last four years, followed by a competence test in countries such as the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Switzerland, Australia and South Africa. Services include furniture construction, door and window installation, flooring, stair construction and structural framing. In the United Kingdom, carpentry describes first-fix work such as roofs and floors, and second-fix items such as doors and windows are generally regarded as carpentry; off-site manufacture of such items is called joinery.

Textile floor covering consisting of a pile layer attached to a backing. The terms carpet and rug are often used interchangeably, though rugs are generally smaller and loose-laid. In Europe the pile was traditionally wool, but since the 20th century synthetic fibers such as [[Polypropylene|polypropylene]], [[Nylon|nylon]] and [[Polyester|polyester]] have been used as less expensive alternatives. Carpets provide cushioning and better sound and heat insulation than tile or stone. They are made by weaving, tufting, hand-knotting, needle felting and embroidery, among other methods. Tufting accounts for over 95% of output in the United States. The oldest surviving carpet is the Pazyryk carpet, dating from the 5th century BC, which was found in a frozen Scythian tomb in the [[Altai Mountains]] of Siberia.

Two- or four-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle for passengers. A coach is an enclosed carriage with four corner posts and a fixed roof. From the [[Early modern period|early modern period]] until railways and motor vehicles displaced them, carriages were a principal means of road transport, including elaborate ceremonial coaches used by royalty. The coach, developed in the 15th and 16th centuries, was lighter and faster, and by the late 16th century had spread across Europe as a standard vehicle for aristocratic and long-distance travel. From the 17th to the 19th centuries, innovations including steel springs, glazing and the fifth wheel made coaches more comfortable and safer. Carriages remain in use for ceremonial occasions, tourism, equestrian sport and, in some communities, everyday transport.

American actress and writer. Fisher played Princess Leia in the original [[Star Wars]] films (1977–1983) and reprised the role in *The Force Awakens* (2015) and *The Rise of Skywalker* (2019). She wrote the semi-autobiographical novel *Postcards from the Edge* and the screenplay for its film version, and the nonfiction book *Wishful Drinking*. She spoke publicly about her [[Bipolar disorder|bipolar disorder]] and drug addiction. She died of sudden cardiac arrest four days after a medical emergency during a transatlantic flight.

Biennial root vegetable in the umbellifer family Apiaceae. The carrot, *Daucus carota* subsp. *sativus*, is a domesticated form of the wild carrot, which is native to Europe and Southwestern Asia. It probably originated in [[Iran]], where it was cultivated for its leaves and seeds. Carrots are typically orange because of β-carotene, a source of vitamin A. Heirloom varieties may be white, yellow, red, purple or black. In 2022, world production of carrots combined with turnips topped 42 million tonnes, with China producing 44% of the total. During the Second World War, a myth that carrots helped people see in the dark was spread as propaganda to explain British pilots' night fighting; the real explanation was [[Radar|radar]].

Two-wheeled vehicle designed for transport, pulled by people or draft animals. Carts may be pulled by [[Horse|horses]], [[Donkey|donkeys]], mules, [[Ox|oxen]], goats or large dogs. Carting is the transport of goods by horse-drawn cart, particularly heavy loads such as coal. The word has come to mean nearly any small conveyance, regardless of its number of wheels or means of propulsion. The earliest known wheels date to around 3400–3000 BC, and the combination of [[Wheel|wheel]] and axle transformed human mobility and trade. Two-wheeled carts required about 40% less pulling force than four-wheeled vehicles of the same weight. With the domestication of oxen and horses, carts became central to ancient economies for farming, trade and migration.

Port city (pop., 2018: 876,885), capital of Bolívar Department, northern Colombia. Known since the imperial era as Cartagena de Indias, the city was founded on June 1, 1533, although indigenous settlement in the area dates from 4000 BC. As a Spanish colony it was a key port for exporting Bolivian silver to Spain and for the [[Atlantic slave trade|import of enslaved Africans]] under the asiento system. Its walls and fortresses defended it against pirates. Its colonial walled city and fortress were designated a [[World Heritage Site]] by [[UNESCO]] in 1984. The city was the site of the Battle of Cartagena de Indias in 1741, during the War of Jenkins' Ear. Today its economy depends on the maritime and petrochemical industries and on tourism.

Coordinate system using perpendicular axes, named for René Descartes. Each point in a plane is specified by two real-number coordinates, the signed distances from two fixed perpendicular axes that meet at the origin, (0, 0). Three coordinates specify a point in three-dimensional space, and *n* coordinates specify a point in *n*-dimensional Euclidean space. [[René Descartes]] published the idea in 1637 in *La Géométrie*, allowing geometric problems to be expressed in algebra and calculus. [[Pierre de Fermat]] independently discovered it but did not publish. The use of a pair of axes followed the Latin translation of *La Géométrie* in 1649. The system is the foundation of [[Analytic geometry]] and the most common coordinate system in [[Computer graphics]]. A circle of radius 2 centered at the origin is described by x² + y² = 4.

Ancient Phoenician city in what is now Tunisia, on the eastern side of the Lake of Tunis. The legendary Phoenician queen Dido is regarded as its founder, though her historicity has been questioned. Carthage developed from a Phoenician colony into the capital of a Punic empire that dominated large parts of the southwestern Mediterranean during the first millennium BC. It was one of the most important trading hubs of the ancient Mediterranean. The Roman Republic destroyed the city in 146 BC, after a siege of nearly three years during the [[Punic Wars|Third Punic War]]. It was rebuilt about a century later as the major city of the Roman province of Africa. Scholars disagree about whether child sacrifice was practiced there, a question raised by excavations in the 1920s. The ruins are a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site.

Resilient, smooth and semi-transparent [[Connective tissue|connective tissue]]. It is usually covered by a tough, fibrous membrane called the perichondrium. In tetrapods it covers the ends of long bones at joints as articular cartilage, and it forms parts of the rib cage, neck, bronchial tubes and intervertebral discs. It is not as hard as [[Bone|bone]], but it is much stiffer than [[Muscle|muscle]] or [[Tendon|tendon]]. Its matrix contains glycosaminoglycans, proteoglycans and collagen fibers. Because cartilage has no blood vessels or nerves, its cells receive nutrients by diffusion. It is classified as elastic, hyaline or fibrocartilage. Its limited capacity for repair makes conditions such as [[Osteoarthritis|osteoarthritis]] a significant clinical concern.

Study and practice of making and using maps. Cartography combines science, aesthetics and technique to model reality, or an imagined reality, in ways that communicate spatial information. Its traditional tasks include selecting the traits of a mapped object, representing its terrain on flat media through [[Map projection|map projections]], generalizing irrelevant characteristics and designing the map to convey its message. The oldest surviving world maps come from Babylonia in the 9th century BC. In the 2nd century AD, [[Ptolemy]] wrote the *Geographia*, which contained his world map. Su Song's star maps in *Xin Yi Xiang Fa Yao* (1092) are the oldest surviving star maps in printed form. Modern cartography underlies [[Geographic information system|geographic information systems]].

Type of two-dimensional visual art, typically drawn in an unrealistic or semi-realistic style. The term first described a full-size preparatory drawing on heavy paper for a painting, fresco, tapestry or stained glass window. Cartoons for frescoes were pricked along their outlines, so that soot pounced through them transferred the design to wet plaster. Since *Punch* applied the term to satirical drawings in 1843, it has referred to humorous or satirical drawings in magazines and newspapers. Cartoons are divided into gag cartoons, which include editorial cartoons, and comic strips. Sir John Tenniel, illustrator of *Alice's Adventures in Wonderland*, contributed over two thousand cartoons to *Punch* over more than 50 years. In the early 20th century the term also came to refer to animated films.
